speechtext: Another Jimmy Gardiner.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
Jimmy Gardiner couldn't hold a candle to these boys. First, the minister said he knew nothing about a letter of intent and he sidestepped like a ballet dancer. If a regulatory body in the United States has knowledge of this letter, and if this government felt they had to get their hands into the deal, why tell an untruth about it? Did the government tell Mr. Brown to keep the letter secret? Did the government tell Ashland that they had to keep the letter secret? They are like boys who paddle on a lake, become so involved in what they are doing that they fall in beyond their depth, and because they can't swim they drown. Mr. Speaker, this government is drowning. The government got themselves involved when they prevented Canadian investors matching foreign offers. That explains their silence and, indeed, their deceit.
It is suggested that it was the imposition of silence on Mr. Brown and Ashland that caused the trouble. Mr. Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company Brown now says that he is in trouble with the securities commission of the United States as a result of the letter of intent, because the government and the minister got their hands ino the deal but refused to act. I hold in my hand the transcript of a great interview held on the program "Question Period" on February 8. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was interviewed by Peter Stursberg, Don Newman and Douglas Fisher. The host was Max Keeping. One of the interviewers asked this question:
But in the case of Denison Mines a year ago you moved in to prohibit it and now you're backing it up with legislation. Why not with the oil industry?
I do not know where the minister stands on this question. Surely, if the industry is entitled to know anything it is entitled to know where the government stands on the constitutional question, in order that investor confidence may be maintained. As the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Douglas) so ably said, the government talks about uranium as coming under the Constitution because it is a public work for the good of Canada. If we can do this with respect to one industry, why cannot we do it with respect to oil? What is the government's position on the constitutional law in this respect? On this question I would have thought the government would have sought advice from the law officers of the Crown and that it would have been forewarned about its powers in this regard. The present uncertainty is killing investment. Canadians cannot obtain dollars for the purchasing of the controlling interest in Home Oil or any other company that is up for sale in this land.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
In this interview the minister gave the following answer to a question:
Q: Isn't the sale imminent though? Is not the sale of Home Oil imminent?
A: Well, the discussions have been going on for some time and I think it's imminent but I am confident that the continuing good will of the parties, buyers and seller, that we can work out a method whereby this company will continue to be Canadian without having to resort to-
This is the question I should like to ask: Is this fair? For how long will American buyers continue to come up here and make offers if every time offers are made with respect to companies such as Home Oil we say, "We want a Canadian company to buy this company at that price." The Americans are pretty tough businessmen and they are not used to being treated as donkeys in this country. If they make an offer, they want to know that they have the right to have it accepted. I say that one must show good faith.
In this country there ought to be priorities and guidelines with respect to tax incentives. If we had such priorities and guidelines, Canadians would voluntarily move into the field. Canadians ought to be given encouragement to enter the field. Our chartered banks should loosen their policies and lend money to Canadians so that our people can develop our resources and our enterprises can participate in development equally with the Ameri-

February 18, 1971
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company cans. After all, Americans borrow Canadian dollars; therefore, why cannot Canadians borrow Canadian dollars?
At least in the banking business the people concerned know where they stand. They know that so many shares must be held by Canadians and how many may be held by foreign investors. Unless we change our tax structure and taxation attitudes we shall kill investor confidence; we shall kill our investment business, kill our resources business and kill development. You will kill the possibility of Canadians owning their own corporations.
I could read more from the interview to which I referred. The minister finally said, "You know, we must create jobs for Canadians." We know we must create jobs. Yet the government's white paper on taxation has scared the development industry to such an extent that people are being laid off. That is what is happening.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: The government is creating unemployment.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
The minister claims that present policies will benefit the little man. Are they good for the little man when he finds himself without work? I think he would rather pay taxes and keep his job. The effect of the white paper on tax reform has been to create unemployment. The white paper has taken away the little man's job and put him on the street. Mr. Speaker, this debate is taking place at a critical time for our economy. We are clearly getting less from our economy than we would like to get from it. While the evidence is that we are on the path toward a better economic performance, it is obvious to the victims of inflation to the victims of unemployment and to the victims, in international trade terms, of our very hard dollar, that we have a fair distance to go.
The Home Oil issue reflects the new dimension of the demands we are making on our economy a problem we have been sweeping under the rug for decades. I regret that the hon. member who just spoke did not acknowledge that the government which he supported swept the problem under the rug as much as Liberal governments in the past.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
Traditionally we have asked our economy to provide us with full employment, reasonable price stability, steady growth, a satisfactory balance of international payments and a fair distribution of the benefits of growth. However, a growing number of Canadians now recognize that even if we achieve all these things we may not have an economy which satisfies our aspirations. We might have a high standard of living and yet be a derivative economy, relying on another country for our direction. We might have industrial development but all geared to foreign input of technology, research and development.
We might have an economy whose activity is assembling parts and implementing ideas shipped to us from abroad, accepting styles of life and goods created elsewhere. All this can happen while our standard of living continues to rise. If that happens, Mr. Speaker, we should not be surprised if our brightest and most able people go to the source country to find jobs which are challenging, fun and offer opportunities to become creators of economic events. If these people leave us for these reasons, what will happen to the rest of Canada's life? How will this affect our culture and national identity?
Such an economy and such a destiny would be unacceptable to me and, I believe, to most Canadians. We can consider the remote example of the American revolution. A factor in that revolution was taxation without representation. Another, and perhaps more important, was the resistance of the American people to the shaping of their economy, by imperial policy, into colonial subser-
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company vience to the mother economy. The revolutionary analogy breaks down, however, because in Canada we already have the political power. How shall it be used?
On the one hand, we want foreign capital if it will increase our standard of living and bring us, as well, know-how, innovation, technology and market access which will permit us to market better products more efficiently. On the other hand, we want to see in our economy the development of a unique identity, a dynamic autonomy, an internal generative power which can push us ahead of other nations in efficiency, creativity, technology and economic style-setting.
We like to refer to the natural resources of Canada as a stock of untold riches. They are riches, as are our vast resources of timber, fertile land and a strong, healthy and industrious people. However, these riches should not be confused with capital. Without capital, resources lie unused. Capital is not resources but command over resources, a means to exploit resources, power to bring them into the market place and the economy.
A national commitment is required to elaborate an economic strategy to achieve these goals. We are told that the development of the strategy is under way in cabinet. It is long overdue. I cannot attemp here to formulate the strategy myself, except to note that it will not be simple and will have to reflect a variety of interests. However, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of assessing the Home Oil question, I believe one obvious limitation exists which, I submit, should assist the government in dealing with the difficult question which must be resolved on an urgent basis.
The proposal I wish to make stems from the observation that Canadian capital will always be in shorter supply than we would like in order to achieve all possible economic goals. We are going to have to choose the areas which are to be protected from foreign investment. How should we decide which to protect? Operating from this premise, I submit that the natural resource industries are the last which should be protected from foreign encroachment. I make this observation recognizing that the general public view tends to be the opposite. The public seems to believe there is some special national interest which requires the exclusion of foreigners from resource development. This may be an elaboration of the territorial imperative but it is a public sentiment which I very much regret.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, the products of the basic natural resource industry contribute very little, if anything, to the Canadian life-style. What is our lifestyle? In the material sense it is our books, food, clothing, educational and entertainment systems, homes, buildings, art and our transportation systems. These are the material things which will make Canadians unique in physical terms, if anything will. I believe a policy of Canadian identity should stress these areas. By contrast, the production of the natural resource industries are neutral international goods devoid of personality. Clearly, the national identity of the owner has a remote impact, if any, on the character of production.
There is a second, more compelling reason why foreign ownership of the natural resource industry represents no

February 18, 1971
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company threat to Canadian identity. There is no industry in which government control can be so effective and complete, irrespective of ownership. A natural resource investment once made is captive, even hostage in a way that no other industry is, to national policy.
Contrast a mining operation on the one hand with an advanced electronic business, typically an international corporation, on the other. The development work of the mining company must be done here physically. For the electric company it can be done in thin air, in a foreign country or in mid-Atlantic. In typical international electronic companies, no single product is made wholly in one country. Even a simple electric razor, typewriter or radio is a multinational product. The offshore operation provides the only market and often the principal supplier of a Canadian branch.
Against such an operation, national priorities of any particular host government are marginal. The international corporation's bargaining position is excellent. It is true that the Canadian plant and equipment may be hostage, but such assets are useless without the rest of the international operation.
A basic natural resource industry, by contrast, is all here. The government priorities must be accepted. There is no bargaining position except future investment which, as it chooses, the government can welcome or not. The labour policies and standards such as the employment of native personnel, degrees of processing, pricing, including a two-price system, export permits which permit embargoes, are all within the power of the host government and, in fact, have all been imposed by federal and provincial governments of Canada in varying degrees. In fact, all these measures I have been describing have been imposed by federal and provincial governments in varying degrees in recent times.
I wish the minister well in his search for a Canadian customer for Home Oil. All Canadians wish him well. If it works, everyone will be happy. If he is unsuccessful, I urge the government to consider buying the company either for the Crown or to offer to the CDC when it is established. But I deeply hope no action will be taken which would lead international mining investors to steer around Canada. This country does not need, and cannot afford, such a policy.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is now studying the problem of the sale of Home Oil to American interests through the transfer of the shares held by Mr. Brown, the main shareholder, to an American.
This problem, Mr. Speaker, which the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas), brought up shows us the need for a Canadian economic policy. To get the picture, let us remember that Home Oil is the main Canadian oil producer. Indeed, it is the most important independent Canadian oil company. It has assets of over $240 million. Home Oil sells more than 350 million gallons of liquid oil annually, and holds about 10 per cent of

the shares of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. It is now a proposal of sale to the American Ashland Oil Company for $10 million.
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that Cygnus Corporation now owns 43.5 per cent of the shares of Home Oil, and that Mr. R. A. Brown holds in his own name 50.3 per cent of the share of Cygnus Corporation. The reason for the sale is that Mr. Brown, the president of Home Oil, has now short-term debts of $90 million and he must pay more than $200,000 in monthly interests on that loan. He apparently borrowed $24 million payable on demand from the Bank of Nova Scotia and over $1,431,000 from the Imperial Bank of Commerce of Canada. Finally, Mr. Brown controls Home Oil since 1952. That is to say that this truly Canadian oil company has been operating in Canada since 1952. I must say "operating", because according to available information which moreover is at variance with the position of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), it seems that this company is no longer Canadian.
The minister insists that he offered some kind of pious opposition to the American Securities Commission, because that transaction would not be acceptable to the Canadian government, but if we refer to his answers during the question period today, obviously, these sessions of "fancy skating" will last for quite a while yet.
If we put this particular problem in a Canadian context, we must realize that presently, more than 87 per cent of Canadian oil and gas producers are in the hands of foreign interests. Thus, 99 per cent of refineries are foreign-owned. What is Canadian in the oil industry? Capital? No. Management? Neither. In fact, the greatest part of the oil industry in Canada belongs to foreign interests. What we have, in Canada, are natural resources that we beg foreigners to come and develop for us, because we lack the capital needed to do it ourselves. We are always faced with the same basic problem, that of Canadian capital.
Mr. Speaker, for a long time in Quebec, we have been told that while we were learning how we had been defeated on the Plains of Abraham, in English Canada people were taught that 2 plus 2 makes 4, plus so much per cent interest. It was said to be a valid explanation of the reason why Quebec did not belong to Quebecers and American capital controlled the province.
The same thing applies to natural resources. As far as Quebec is concerned, it will be remembered that a premier by the name of Duplessis gave away the iron ore of the province to Americans for a mess of pottage, begging them to process it in secondary industries so that we may buy it back at high prices.
Today's policy is not new. For too long in Canada we have left to others the task of developing our own natural resources so that today, if we place the Home Oil problem in the overall picture, we realize that the situation has become very serious. Home Oil is a Canadian business in the process of becoming American. That is the tragedy, and it is not new. Slowly but surely, our leaders-if one can call them that since their leadership does not extend over much and since all our raw materials
February 18, 1971

belong to foreigners-have let foreigners take over our basic industries.
This vast country, which at one time belonged to us, does not belong to us now. We have become tenants. A tenant should not be asked to boast of the values and qualities of a house that no longer belongs to him. That is why I am so surprised by the speech made by the hon. member who preceded me, who talked of the pride of being Canadians, who sang the praise of Canadian unity, or of this vast country that is described in picture books.
Mr. Speaker, that is a stupid policy, because the country no longer belongs to us. It did at one time, but today it belongs to foreigners.
Mr. Speaker, it is no wonder that Canadians take no pride whatsoever in being Canadians, because all they get in Canada is taxes. Their lot is to be hustled by the government which, wittingly and knowingly, sold Canada down the river to the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I shall quote precise figures, and I must point out that since they were published in 1967, the situation has been getting worse.
In the soft drinks industry, 26 per cent of interests was in foreign hands and 14 per cent under foreign control.
The rubber industry was 88 per cent in foreign-owned and 99 per cent foreign-controlled.
"The minister with the smile", Jean-Luc Pepin, boasts about the fact that we have a Canadian textile industry but, Mr. Speaker, he was one of those who gave this industry away, for 24 per cent of shares are in foreign hands and 23 per cent under foreign control.
In the pulp and paper industry, 51 per cent of shares are in foreign hands and 46 per cent under foreign control.
In the farm machinery industry, 47 per cent of shares are in foreign hands and 54 per cent under foreign control.
In the automobile industry, 90 per cent of shares are in foreign hands and 97 per cent under foreign control.
In the transport equipment industry, 58 per cent of shares are in foreign hands and 71 per cent under foreign control.
The same applies to electrical appliances, iron and steel, oil and natural gas and the mining industry.
As for oil and natural gas, 87 of shares are in foreign hands.
I was aware, a few minutes ago, of a dispute between the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), who were giving each other tit for tat, asking which of them was responsible, through inertia, for the sale of Canadian interests to foreigners.
Mr. Speaker, the figures I have just cited are by no means heartening. I recall that during the 1957 and 1958 election campaigns, the right hon. member for Prince Albert travelled the country and stated dramatically and
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company bombastically "Canada to Canadians", all for the evident purpose of getting votes.
From 1957 to 1961, with the Conservative administration, foreign ownership increased from 54 to 56 per cent, and foreign control jumped from 61 to 64 per cent.
The Liberals may think it funny because it suits their purpose, but they were in power themselves from 1935 to 1957. Were they more Canadian than the Conservatives? They may well say that they achieved unity, that they were the only ones to do so, but the fact still remains that they had some shady role in that. The Liberals were first responsible for the U.S. take-over of our economy. When I see them crying and apologizing today, it reminds me of crocodile tears. Their wailing sounds remind me of bleating sheep happy to be shorn by the Americans and going "baa .. . baa ... baa ..."
In 1935, 37 per cent of our economy as well as 45 per cent of our mining industry belonged to foreigners. After 20 years of Liberal administration, in the name of the famous economic liberalism, men like the hon. Walter Gordon, who advocated a nationalistic economic policy, were expulsed from the party because, as they were saying, that upsets our projects. Yet, this man was a Canadian. They preferred selling Canadians to the United States rather than keeping Canadian people in the Liberal party.
After 20 years of Liberal administration, foreigners controlled more than 56 per cent of our industries. Indeed, 80 per cent of the capital controlling us is American capital. That is saying a good deal.
We can almost hear already the pompous speeches that will be delivered by eloquent government members to say nothing. The situation will nevertheless be tolerated and the Home Oil Company will fall into American hands. Why? Because the Canadian government has no national economic policy, because it discourages the investment of Canadian capital, because it puts out white papers like the one on fiscal reform for instance, which prevents Canadians from investing their profits in the Canadian economy.
The government wants to tax and discourage the Canadian people. Home Oil will fall into American hands because this government is the Americans' pay instead of being at the service of the Canadian people. Home Oil will be taken over by the Americans because the Canadian government is controlled by high finance and not by the Canadian people.
That is why I am convinced that Home Oil will fall into American hands and that again the development of our natural resources will be left to others. And yet, it would be so easy to develop a Canadian economic policy, a development policy for our natural resources, a policy that would enable us to invite young Canadians, particularly the 45 per cent of the unemployed under 25, to bring in their contribution. They are quite willing to participate in the building of their country but if the government continues to boost unemployment with their phony fight against inflation while giving away our natural resources, we shall not have to wonder why young Canadians do not believe any more in Canada. Therefore, it should be understood that Canadians want a truly

February 18, 1971
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company
Canadian government. One would wonder whether this government is not an American government.
Mr. Speaker, this situation is hopeless. We have several solutions to offer. We could legislate to prevent Home Oil Company from being sold to American interests as has already been done in the case of the selling of Denison Mines to the Hudson Bay Oil & Gas Company last year.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is just smilling as does the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and the others sold to the Americans. The first one remains idle and contents himself with denying, and pretending he knows nothing. If a minister knows nothing, this is a serious situation.
Here is a solution. I do not suggest it is the best but if this government is truly Canadian they will quickly find a solution so that Home Oil Company will remain Canadian as has been done for Denison Mines.
I would like to offer another solution to the minister. The choice will be his. Since he does not seem to have any idea, then I will give him one. The government itself could buy Home Oil Company and later sell it to Polymer Corporation or to the Canada Development Corporation.
That is another solution but it is not pleasing because it is tinted with socialism. If the government takes over private enterprise, that does not please me. I say it again: That solution is tinted with socialism.
It would be better if that company became a crown corporation with a mixed economy, which would permit to buy back the shares of Home Oil, instead of seeing the company fall into American hands. That solution would be a poultice on a wooden leg, but at least a Canadian poultice.
Mr. Speaker, in one thing at least I am different from the leader of the New Democratic party; he does not make any distinction between crown corporations, because he dreams of socialism, while I hope at least that that corporation will have a mixed economy, so that it would be possible to invite Canadian investors to contribute, by their capital, to the management of that new corporation, which could be advised by the Polymer Corporation.
Mr. Speaker, a third solution could be considered. I do not deem it excellent in itself, but it is a possible solution that might allow the Canadian people to keep their own resources.
That third solution be the following: the government would vouch for the liabilities of the Home Oil Company. I believe that this would be the best answer.
Mr. Speaker, the main problem of Mr. Brown, president of Home Oil, is that considering the existing fiscal system, he had to borrow tremendous amounts of money and must pay in interest fees only over $200,000 per month. Such liabilities that he can no longer meet because he is now being stifled by high finance, the latter enjoying the Canadian government's protection, of course, compel him to sell Home Oil to Americans. All this is happening because the government does not control the Canadian economy. Why could it not guarantee the debts of the Home Oil Company? This would prevent it from selling itself to Americans.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government grants interest-free loans to foreign countries, for instance, India. Up to now, over $201 million have been loaned to India, interest-free, for a 60-year period. This means that the Canadian government is guaranteeing the development of that country.
Not long ago, our right hon. national traveller, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), at a cost of many millions of dollars, visited that country on behalf of the Canadian people, whereas we were still involving ourselves into new debts and were still being crushed under the weight of interest charges. For his part, he went around, strutting like a peacock and leaving behind here and there millions of dollars, interest free and refundable over a 60-year period, while the Canadian people were crushed under financial obligations. Such loans were granted for the development of those countries, to spare them the fate of the Middle East countries, as was stated by the leader of the New Democratic Party, where resources are almost wholly foreign-owned.
This government grants interest-free loans to some countries to help them develop and control their own resources while, at the same time, it crushes Canadians. It does absolutely nothing to save Canadian industry and provokes through inertia and lethargy the sell-out of Canadian enterprises to American hands.
Mr. Speaker, we of the Ralliement Creditiste strongly advocate an economic policy that would give back Canadian industries to Canadians through the use of credit based on the real credit of the nation. Natural resources do not belong either to the ome Oil Company or to the Americans, but to all Canadians. Natural resources do not belong either to the Home Oil Company do not belong to a Canadian in particular, not anymore than to the present Prime Minister or to the right hon. member for Prince Albert-the two persons who sold us out-but to all Canadians. It is the government's duty to give these natural resources back to Canadians through a national economic policy and it should guarantee the Home Oil debts.

Mr. Speaker, I hoped to follow the minister. Since this is a debate which has been called on the basis of urgency, I thought the minister would speak after the lead-off speakers of the three opposition parties had had their say, if only to indicate the government's position. This matter is of enormous concern to this country and it is important that we know the government's intention. I suggest there is more involved in this question than just the Home Oil Company. We must put this in the context of what is happening internationally in order to assess its importance and the importance of having in Canada a company which does not react to and depend upon the international oil situation.
For years the major oil companies of the world have been able to play the interests of one oil producing nation against another. There has been a long pattern of James Bond intrigue. By following this pattern these companies have been able to assure control of international oil markets. The only exception has been in respect of countries like Italy and others in Europe which got into the oil business on their own. The oil producing nations of the world decided to get together to counter this kind of international activity on the part of oil companies. We are now faced with a situation in this country, or will be shortly, that is faced by other countries which do not have oil, do not have conservation policies and do not control the oil industries which exist. We will soon find ourselves blackmailed as well, not only by our national oil companies but by the international companies.
This fact points out the importance of maintaining strong Canadian participation in our oil industry. The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) suggested that the government could regulate this industry. We have observed a long history of this type of regulation by government in respect of the gas and oil industry. After looking at the record in this regard we can decide that the National Energy Board has been the patsy of the oil companies. The oil companies have won every round in this battle.

speechtext:
They are the ones who sit idly by while this country is sold out. I challenge the minister to rise tonight and tell us about his plan to do something about the oil industry in Canada. I had intended to point out what had taken place before the inception of the National Energy Board. After 1966, following a long debate in this House about a natural gas pipe line, the government decided to provide a route through the United States but attached some conditions. Now, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is not delivering the amount of gas required in Canada in spite of its promises at that time. There was a package deal arranged which allowed for an increase in the amount delivered on the basis of a higher price. This is what the companies want. That is not what was decided in 1966.
How does the government propose to untangle this mess? I suggest that the problem will be resolved in the usual way, with the oil companies getting what they want. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams) referred to the oil industry in relation to the white paper on taxation. The white paper has not been implemented and has not been discussed for some time. Why has the oil industry in Canada been sold out to United States interests? It has been suggested that this has some connection with the tax structure. I suggest it has not happened because of taxes. The amount of tax paid by the oil industry in Canada has been decreasing. If we look at the documentation in Walter Gordon's book "Choice for Canada" we see how much in taxes the oil companies have contributed to Canada. So it is not a problem of taxes. Taxes on the oil industry will not change anything.
The truth of the matter is that a Canadian company, limited to its own resources, cannot compete economically in the international cartelization that goes in the world today. For years Home Oil has come to the Canadian people and the Canadian government and said, "Build a pipe line to Montreal. Give us a chance. If you do not, we will be stuck with the internationals who allocate where the oil goes and does not go". We have refused the pipeline to Montreal. Why? Is it because it is uneconomic? In the oil industry we do not talk about uneconomic things. The oil industry is political from start to finish. The international oil policy is political.

February 18, 1971
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company
The national oil policy was designed on the basis that whatever offshore crude the Canadian oil displaced in the United States, mid-west markets would be taken in at Montreal. For many years we asked in this House about a national oil policy. We asked if such a deal had been made and if this was part of the policy. No one was willing to say, until one day the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) blurted it out; then everyone was aware of it. I do not know whether he blurted it out or was a little more honest than others; I suspect he was a little more honest.
The point is that you cannot separate oil from politics. Talk about economics does not make sense. My leader made the mildest proposals tonight. He suggested that as an immediate course we should do something to make sure this oil company is not sold out to the Americans. We are not talking about public or private ownership. We need at least one company in Canada which has a sense of obligation to the Canadian public instead of to a great big club around the world known as the international oil cartel.
Home Oil, whatever its difficulties and attitudes may be-and we are not particularly lovers of the oil industry-has a voice that is Canadian. The appeal it made to this government was that it have a voice with the international oil companies. Why did they want the pipeline to Montreal? They commissioned a very extensive study for that purpose because they were the only ones with a big interest in having a pipeline to Montreal. The internationals did not care; it did not make any difference to them whether they sold oil from Venezuela, Arabia or Alberta. What was the sense of pushing Canadian oil if they could send Venezuelan crude here?
There have been a number of studies in respect of the peipeline. I know of three. The one the oil companies commissioned was a study by W. J. Levy Inc., entitled "Outlook for Canadian Crude Production and Markets". In examining the pipeline proposal to Montreal it suggested it was not a good idea. One reason is that the internationals would cut our price to make sure we could not sell oil at any price but theirs. They are quite capable of doing this because their profit margins are high enough. So whatever price we could deliver to Montreal would be cut.
P. S. Auf Der Maur conducted an extensive study in 1968. He pointed out the advantages of bringing western crude to Montreal. He said there is a pollution factor involved and Canadian crude is much purer in the sense that you do not have to refine it extensively in order to make it pollution free. He stated it is a better type of oil for that reason. But again price enters the picture. There was a study commissioned by the department of research and development of Canadian National Railways entitled, "Some Implications of Marketing Canadian Crude in Montreal". It showed that at that time the differential, even given the posted price of oil at Montreal, as against western crude brought in by a private pipe line to Montreal was 28 cents a barrel. That is not a great difference when one considers that with the increase that will inevitably take place in respect of international crude prices, the 28 cents a barrel would be wiped out.
It would seem to me, aside from the immediate problem, we should be ensuring that we are not put at the mercy of offshore oil and are not placed in the position of being blackmailed in this respect. Let us remember one thing. This does not mean that the price of Canadian oil or gasoline will be cheaper west of Montreal. At the moment it is supposed to be a little cheaper west of Ottawa. But I am quite convinced the Canadian oil producers will waste no time in raising their prices to match international prices at the moment.
When we are talking about a pipe line I should like to put on record the significant difference between a publicly-owned pipe line and a privately-owned pipe line. One of the greatest mistakes ever made in the history of our country was letting the Trans-Canada pipe line be built by private people rather than by the government. We have paid a terrible price ever since that dreadful decision. I should like to refer to the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Committee on Industry, Research and Energy Development, for June 21, 1966.
Mr. McKinnon was before the committee and was asked whether he had studied the cost of moving western crude to Montreal. He was asked what it would cost to move a barrel of crude from the west to Montreal. He asked whether this would be done privately or publicly, because it would appear that if it were done privately the cost would probably be between 60 cents and 70 cents but if it were done publicly the cost would be 50 cents a very significant difference. This seemed to be a very compelling argument for a publicly-owned pipe line.
What, then, do we do tonight? If I know the minister, he loves to evade answers. Very often he makes great political speeches. He made one last year at the Liberal convention which did not do him much good but got him a lot of applause. I am sure he is lurking around somewhere with a pad and pencil and that instead of telling us what his government will do he will say the Conservatives want us to do one thing, the NDP want something else, the Creditistes something different and Mr. Salts-man wants something else. We are not in a position to make proposals. It should not be of very much concern to him that all of us have different ideas about what should be done.
One thing is obvious in this House tonight. Everyone on this side recognizes the vital importance of Home Oil Company remaining in Canadian hands in some way, whether by tax concessions or some other way. All of us are concerned that something be done, and we will not be pawned off by any sort of juvenile trick the minister may have up his sleeve. I would make a suggestion that I think has some merit, because in the long run simply selling Home Oil to another Canadian company would not solve the problem. It would give us some breathing space, which is important, and therefore I am in favour of it. It would give us the time we need to look at the situation. However, I do not think it would solve the problem because I do not believe a Canadian company, dependent on its own resources and financing, will ever be able to compete with the kind of dominance achieved by the international giants in the oil industry.

February 18, 1971

This is the kind of thing the Canadian Development Corporation could do. I think the Canadian government must ensure that if a Canadian buyer is not found, the government itself will become that buyer, because in the long run control of oil and politics are the same. The hon. member who spoke earlier felt that it was not very important whether or not we got into the natural resource industries. He could think of some things that were much better, and he tended to pooh-pooh the importance of the oil industry. Let me remind the hon. member that these natural resources vitally affect us in this country because today oil is the primary product in the textile industry. It is the base for the chemical world in which we live.
Oil, and who controls oil, determine to a very large extent what kind of measures will be taken regarding our environment in terms of pollution and things related to it. It vitally affects our life-style. It is true that governments have the power to regulate the industry but it is not true that there is any evidence that the Liberal party has ever used that power or is willing to use it. Their ideological hang-up, their commitment to the market is so strong that they can only react when faced with an immediate disaster.
The only time the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) acted precipitously was with reference to Denison Mines. I hope he does so now, but time is short. Why do we have to wait until we are on the edge of the cliff, ready to fall off, before someone throws us a rope? Surely this matter could have been anticipated. Surely it was obvious what was happening in the industry and plans could have been made, instead of the fooling around that is going on at this time. Therefore, I would suggest that under no circumstances should Home Oil Company be permitted to fall into foreign hands. The government must come up with an answer that will ensure this company remains in Canadian hands, so we can have a base of some kind and a Canadian voice of some kind, or the government of Canada itself, on behalf of the people of Canada, should purchase Home Oil.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alastair Gillespie (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the one thing which this House recognizes tonight is the importance of the issue we are discussing. I do not think there is any question that the members of this House are speaking and reflecting on a matter of major concern to Canadians, and I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate this evening.
I think Canadians all across this country are asking themselves whether yet another Canadian corporation is to go the way that so many already have gone. We all know that over the last eight years hundreds of Canadian firms have been taken over in the absence of any national or provincial policies in this area, and perhaps many thinking Canadians are asking what chance there is for Canada to maintain its political independence if we stand idly by as one firm after another is taken over by foreign owners. Many of you may have seen in the last
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company week or two figures presented from Colura. Those figures indicated that slightly over 42 per cent of all the corporate profits-that is 42 per cent of the profits of all incorporated firms in Canada-are earned by foreign-controlled firms. In many ways this seems to me to be a more significant figure than the percentage of our foreign-controlled industry.
This evening we are talking about the Home Oil Company in particular, although I think it raises issues far wider, as the previous speaker, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) indicated. As we know, Home Oil is the largest of the independent oil companies left in Canadian hands. Most of us applaud the minister for the sense of commitment he has shown in these negotiations and we wish him well in his efforts. We may question whether he has the power, but we wish him well.
A year ago the expectations of Canadians were raised significantly when the Canadian government stepped in and halted the sale of control to foreign owners of Denison Mines. During this period of a year Canadians have been waiting patiently for a statement of policy in this area. During this period we have seen two of the major remaining textbook publishing firms sold to U.S. owners. As a result of this sale, 95 per cent of all the books used in Canadian elementary and high schools are now published by firms which are controlled by non-Canadians. Only 5 per cent of the books used in Canadian schools today are published by Canadian-controlled firms.
I do not propose to deal with the cultural identity argument this evening although I acknowledge, as did the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) that the question of cultural identity is absolutely central to this issue. But it is not the only issue. Cultural sovereignty is one issue. I would argue that economic sovereignty is another and that they are twin pillars in building and developing an independent Canada. It seems to me that there is every likelihood that in the ensuing months other major or significant Canadian corporations will be faced with a similar situation as that now facing Home Oil Company.
Do we stand idly by agonizing on the sidelines? Do we say that we have not the federal power to deal with the situation? We can, as we did with regard to textbooks, indicate that this is primarily a provincial matter, and I think that is right. But are we to encourage those who would purchase Canadian industry? Are we to clap them on the back, as perhaps Stanley Randal might be prompted to do? His remarks recently have indicated that he would repudiate the position that might be taken by candidates of the Conservative party running for leadership in Ontario, with respect to the question of foreign ownership. I say that we have a major problem and that we cannot afford to sit idly by.
We cannot take decisions by default. There is no question in my mind and I think, as I have already said, that this is reflected in the views of those who have spoken this evening, that the Canadian people are concerned about this matter. Recent Gallup polls published in the newspapers would support this view. Equally, there have

February 18, 1971
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company been Gallup polls supporting a positive and aggressive position for the Canada Development Corporation.
It might well be that Canadians would say, "Why do we not in some way get the Canada Development Corporation to deal with this situation? Isn't this the very situation that the Canada Development Corporation was designed to deal with?" I think the clear answer is no. The Canada Development Corporation is not designed to deal with this kind of situation. I think that this situation, better than anything else, points out the problems when we look at the pre-emptive purchase. Take the situation, for example, of Home Oil. It might be that Home Oil will be worth more to a foreign buyer than to a Canadian buyer because, integrated with other foreign firms, the value of that integration, or the synergetic effect will be worth a premium to a foreign owner. For these reasons, those who have read the Canada Development Corporation legislation will recognize that corporation is not well designed for this kind of situation.
As the hon. member for Waterloo said in his remarks, we are dealing with a subject which is far greater in extent than just the question of one takeover. While I would not agree with his views on what we need in the way of an industrial strategy, I would suggest that broadly speaking we should be considering an industrial strategy for Canada, and foreign ownership is part of such an industrial strategy.
I think the debate this evening has obscured some of the main issues. For instance, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) in his loud and noisy bluster did not distinguish between investment on the one hand and foreign ownership on the other. I think it important, if we are going to deal with this issue, that we make that distinction. Nor, Mr. Speaker, can I agree with all the sentiments of the hon. member for Don Valley when he said he felt the natural resource industry is the last area we should be concerned with when we come to formulating foreign ownership policies. In my view it is one of the first areas we should concern ourselves with, partly because natural resource industries are the dominant industrial group in Canada and partly because they alone have the major opportunity for going multinational, and certainly because they are the industries on which we rely most heavily for our export sales. One might also add it is more likely that the natural resource industries will integrate, and integrate down in such a way that an even larger proportion of Canadian industry will be affected when there is a foreign takeover in a natural resource industry.
So I would say that in considering the issues raised in this debate we should place the need for an industrial policy close to the top, and we should recognize the importance of the multinational corporation in the seventies and beyond. We should see the multinational corporation, not in a defensive way, something to resist, but in the opportunity sense. It seems to me that for too long Canadians have reacted defensively against the multinational corporation. They have seen it not as an opportunity, as it should be, but as a threat.
It might help those who still feel this way to note that 70 per cent of the exports of Canadian subsidiaries of
U.S. corporations are sold or exported to firms which are associated with those subsidiaries. In other words, the flow of trade is not the way it used to be in a commodity sense, but between the subsidiary and the associated companies within the group. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that we need to distinguish the capacity of resource industry to go multinational, and I think in the Home Oil Company we have such an opportunity. It represents for Canada and Canadians an opportunity to build something larger around the last large, independent Canadian corporation.
Similarly, I think we need to distinguish two other aspects when we talk about foreign investment and foreign ownership policies. We need to distinguish on the one hand a general category of new plants, and on the other a different category of existing Canadian plants which may be taken over by foreign owners. Within the new plants category we need to distinguish between the branch plant which is producing a carbon copy of the same item that the parent is making. Surely this is less attractive in terms of long-term policy as an industrial strategy than satellite plants, which I would argue are different. A satellite plant would be a plant manufacturing a component to be exported to the foreign corporation, probably a component which no other corporation within the group is presently manufacturing. Without trouble, one could think of other distinctions. I leave one more with the House-that of autonomous plants which are not necessarily producing components but are producing a product which is viable on its own, which is distinctive and perhaps fits the product line in a complementary way but not necessarily in a complementary way.
Turning now to the category of the takeovers, let me say that I think we need a special policy with respect to takeovers which is distinctive and different from the policies I have been talking about in the areas of investment for new plant and resource industry. I think we need it just as much to protect existing Canadian entrepreneurship as we do to protect our capacity to develop Canadian entrepreneurship in the future. Every time a Canadian firm is taken over the capacity of Canadians to develop a distinctive Canadian enterprise is affected and sometimes eliminated.
In my remarks I have tried to indicate that this whole area is immensely complicated. I have no doubt this is the reason why it has taken so long to produce a foreign ownership policy for Canada. The more one gets into it, the more one realizes the interrelationship and the difficulties. This evening I would like to place before the House several recommendations which I think might help in developing such a policy. When this policy comes down it should contain provisions to protect the control and the ownership-and I think it is important that we distinguish between control and ownership-of existing and potential multinational firms. The Home Oil Company is such a firm. It meets that test: it is a potential multinational corporation within the Canadian scheme of things.

If you had imagination, you would see it had potential. I think we need investment rules with respect to foreign investment and I suggest we should have a rule for future foreign investment of 50 per cent Canadian ownership. I would say to the private sector, make your own deals. Meet the 50 per cent requirement, but make your own deals and, if you cannot get sufficient Canadian partners to go along with you, talk to the Canada Development Corporation. That corporation, I would suggest, would be a very useful instrument in this field of meeting the Canadian content test. It should, of course, consider such a proposal only if it meet the test of profitability.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I, for one, am impressed with the sense of commitment the minister has displayed in dealing with this very difficult problem. I wish that he did not have to rely on his powers of persuasion, which are considerable. I wish that legislation was in being which would enable him and the government to act with expedition. There is, however, no such legislation in this country at this time; nor have I heard any members of the opposition propose the kinds of items which ought to be included in such legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: I argue that our No. 1 priority ought to be the development of a policy which will anticipate the problem that may be raised by the sale of other firms. I urge the government to bring in new policies which would establish takeover rules and, if possible, a mechanism or instrument to deal with takeovers. Other countries such as Australia, the United Kingdom, Japan and France have dealt with this problem. It is high time that we did so. If we do not deal with it now we are very likely to be embarrassed in one month, or two months. In my view, we cannot wait.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak this evening on this motion because I, too, am concerned about the amount of foreign ownership in Canada. I am concerned that the decisions with regard to our resources are not being made by Canadians. The power to make those decisions is being taken out of Canadian hands. These days we hear a great deal of discussion about the quality of life and the standard of living. What those two phrases really mean to me is that we must have some right, some ability, to make decisions that affect our own livelihood and personal well-being.
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company Little by little, as the power to make these decisions slips into the hands of foreign corporations, so slips away the power that Canadians may enjoy in the years ahead to control the quality of their lives.
I think that we need a government inspired by a sense of national mission. Its mission must be to create hope and opportunity for Canadians, so that they may enjoy the highest quality of life possible. I say again that we must have the right to make decisions in the years ahead which will affect the quality of our lives. I do not think the government has shown any willingness to act in a way which will retain Home Oil under Canadian ownership. The previous speaker dealt at length with what the minister has been doing. He hoped the minister will be successful. During the last week or so questions during the oral question period have been directed to the minister on this subject; yet the minister has not explained in any way, shape or form just what is going on or what he hopes to do.

We have sat patiently for two hours this evening watching the minister flit in and out of the House. I expect he will make a speech some time this evening. It would have been a much better debate if the minister had been the first or second participant. Then, we would have known what the government intended to do. But, no, the minister did not do that. I can only conclude that the minister's position is rather weak. He must be quite defenceless against these arguments. He does not want anybody to follow him in the debate. He wants to be the last speaker so he can truthfully say that, after he spoke, nobody made any constructive suggestions; that the opposition had nothing constructive to offer. That is not a good excuse.
The government possesses the facts. It knows who owns the shares, what shares are holding shares and which ones are not. It knows the details of the deal. It is in the best position to recommend some action and to lay before the House the facts of the case. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asked the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), "What would the opposition do?" He seemed to be devoid of ideas. That is how it often appears to me. To me, the government is not displaying leadership. This is a weak government, without imagination; it is not a government that can lead the Canadian people and offer them guidance.
What has been going on in the oil industry during the past number of years? It is plain to anyone who knows the oil industry in this country that that industry needed a large amount of investment capital. One cannot overemphasize the fact that investment in the oil industry involves high risk capital, as anybody who has read Carl Nickle's periodic oil report from Calgary will realize. That report keeps on saying that the oil industry faces uncertain times as the result of federal government tax policies relating to oil exports, and as a result of the federal government changing the rules and regulations applying in the north. I see the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) present in the House; he

February 18, 1971
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company knows what is taking place in the north. He knows that the oil industry faces uncertainties.

speechtext: There have been certain changes.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: The hon. member can make his own speech. His voice is probably in better shape than mine. He knows that the oil industry is not particularly happy about the changes which have taken place. speechtext: In Alaska.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
In Alaska, certainly. I ask, were they encouraged to go into the north? They were not encouraged. The whole industry is in a state of flux. I know the minister went to Denver and made his famous speech, and now the Americans are saying, "Fill your pipelines with Canadian oil. They are saying this because of the situation in the Middle East and because the Arabs want to dictate the price and quantity of oil moving to the western world. That is why the Americans want to fill their pipelines with Canadian oil. It is not because the minister went down there and made a speech in which he severely chastised them for their actions with regard to Canada.
There has been a great deal of talk about the supply of oil in Canada today. There is no doubt about what the white paper will do. I wish to quote from a recent speech of Mr. Robert Bryce which appears in "Canada Month":
Why be upset? asks the former deputy-minister of taxation, Robert Bryce. As he explained in a speech to the civil service, private savings will not be dissipated by the White Paper; they will merely be replaced by public savings.
I suppose this is what the government expects when they start the new company, the Canada Development Corporation. However we must hearken back to what the minister said when he introduced that bill in the House. He said the Corporation will not be used to buy back Canada and it will not be a Corporation of last resort. One wonders how it would help in this particular case. Perhaps the minister will have some enlightening news. Perhaps he has encouraged Panarctic to buy Home Oil.
The whole question of providing leadership to encourage Canadians to own their own resources must be balanced with the question of available money and priorities. Politicians have been talking about priorities for many years. I quote from today's Ottawa Journal:
It will cost the federal treasury about $31.5 million during fiscal 1971-72 to maintain the National Arts Centre, the National Film Board, the National Library, the National Museums and the Public Archives.
I am not saying that money should not be spent. However, here we have a resource, the last major Canadian oil company sliding out of our hands. What efforts are we making? The minister can say that money does not grow on trees. He can say we do not have $10 million because
we must spend $31 million on other things. An article in the same paper is headed:
Language Training To Cost $8.8 Million
It all boils down to what we really think is important. Do we think that Canada's resources should be exploited by companies to a greater extent than they already are or do we think that we can own Canada to any real extent and reap the benefits of these resources by allowing them to slowly slide away? We have to get into the question of regulations and other methods the government can adopt. I quote from an article in today's Globe and Mail:
According to industry and federal sources, existing tax regulations squeezed Home Oil to the point where it cannot but accept a helping hand from the U.S. oil company.
It is a pretty sad situation if we are so madly in search of money that we have to force the last major Canadian oil company out of existence. The doubts about the white paper on taxation has been around for too long. The minister should have clarified the position a long time ago. When asked about certain aspects of the white paper, the minister said the committees were still studying it and he could not say what portions would, or would not remain. Both the committee of this House and the Senate committee have completed their examination of the white paper and made their recommendations to the minister. It would be very easy for the minister to say that certain portions of the white paper will not be implemented. He could have done that six months ago. He could clearly state what he is going to do with the capital gains tax. This also could have been stated six months ago when the committees brought in their recommendations.
The minister has allowed the country to remain in an atmosphere of uncertainty whereby Canadians are not encouraged to invest in Canadian primary industry. When in Saskatchewan last week, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) stated that perhaps we need more Crown corporations in order that enough jobs will be created. Maybe that is what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) has in his hip pocket. If we wait long enough tonight, maybe we will hear about it. These things should have been said some time ago. I personally, do not believe the government cannot employ everyone in Canada. I think the people have to use their own initiative in this country as they have in the past. Last year the Department of Regional Economic Expansion spent $98 million to create a little more than 15,000 jobs. This gives some idea of how much the government can do in that regard. Compared to the 668,000 who are unemployed today, 15,000 or 16,000 jobs is a pretty small drop in the bucket.
The government is not doing enough to encourage Canadians to invest in this country. It is encouraging Canadians to withdraw their savings and put them somewhere else. They will invest in foreign corporations or spend their money on some other aspect of their daily lives. This is a deplorable situation. Canadian corporations have been encouraged to make less profit. In fact, the corporations have made less profit in the last year or

February 18, 1971

so. This has created a situation where the money is not being ploughed back into the industry. They have only earned enough for operating cash.
In a young and growing country, a situation should be created whereby it is not a sin to make a profit. If that profit is ploughed back into raw materials and resources, it will create more jobs. It is interesting to note that in some of his rare moments, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has recognized the fact that profits are not a sin. When he introduced the Canada Development Corporation bill, he said it was for the purpose of investing in companies to make a profit. I understand that the Canada Development Corporation will not be subject to income tax.
We cannot allow companies to make a profit and then take away nearly all that profit through some severe sort of taxation. The companies will flounder and sell out to American firms which get a better tax break. Many Canadian companies are moving their head offices out of Canada because of our tax laws. One member who spoke earlier mentioned international and multinational companies; but it would be a tragedy if the head offices of all these companies were outside Canada. More than one company has moved out. They prefer to pay a 15 per cent tax rather than a 50 or 60 per cent tax.
I will itemize what this government has done wrong in so far as the oil and gas industry is concerned. It has tightened and discouraged the forming of large amounts of investment capital; created an uncertainty with regard to the depletion allowance, and changed the regulations in the north, thus causing great uncertainty. The minister's speech in Denver about the oil and gas industry caused such a kerfuffle that the minister had to go to Calgary to pacify the industry and tell them he was really not that bad a person.
_ Then again, included in the white paper is the suggestion that there should be a capital gains tax, something which would discourage investment in Canadian corporations. Also included in the white paper is a proposal for an evaluation tax on shares. In my opinion, this is an unworkable suggestion and one which will not be implemented, but the minister has not yet wiped the slate clean in this regard. So, the government has proposed a number of things which have resulted in takeovers of companies in every sector of our society and it is time they were put on the mat for their actions in this regard. Canada cannot become the great country it is capable of becoming unless we state a goal and lay down national rules under which the country can develop in an atmosphere of security for investors and of reward for effort. In these circumstances, Canadians would be encouraged to work to save so that they might be in a position to make a greater investment in Canada in the years ahead.

speakeroldname: Mr. Martin P. O'Connell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
My
remarks this evening will be brief, but what I want to say will be in support of the thesis that in no circumstances should we permit the sale of Home Oil to foreign interests. The debate this evening comes at a most oppor-
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company tune time in that it permits the House to give some guidance to the government in a serious dilemma. The dilemma arises partly from the fact that the owners of Home Oil have done nothing wrong. They have broken no laws and there is no legislation to prevent them from selling their company to foreigners. There are no guidelines yet in place. So, the debate comes at an opportune time to enable us to express some views in this area where policy has not yet emerged. As most of us understand, I believe, it will be some months yet before the government is in a position to discuss or to publish guidelines with respect to foreign takeovers. It is incumbent upon us, therefore, to speak our minds on this particular issue and I, for one, find no difficulty in expressing my views.
I should like to allude to what I believe to be a major concern in the minds of people across Canada. This is the concern that in many areas of national life some things are running almost beyond control. I think this feeling is true with respect to pollution. The chemicals being put into the air and the water are so numerous and so complex that we may be going beyond the point of no return. A similar fear arises with respect to urbanization, and the same feeling affects people in connection with the technological revolution, that things are running beyond control and that Parliament is unable to cope with them. I believe we find this feeling, too, over the question of foreign ownership. There is a growing fear that by failing to take the necessary steps when they are clearly called for we are permitting the situation to develop past the point of no return. This becomes a more pressing question for all of us as we stand on the verge of a scientific and technological revolution, the consequences of which we do not clearly foresee.
What concerns people is the thought that we might look back in ten years time and realize that by failing to take steps when we had the opportunity we had gone so far in allowing control of our economy to slip away that we could not reverse the direction of events. This feeling finds its way into the debate on Home Oil, and it will find its way into debates on many other questions involving foreign takeovers since people will see in each particular instance the general spectre of events running out of control, with machinery not yet in place and with a Parliament which does not seem to have the will to take the necessary action.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
We, in this House, are responding to that sort of feeling in the country, but this is not enough guidance in itself for a government which has to take responsibility. And simply to express feelings of this kind would not be a substitute for guidance in this particular case. There would have to be other solid reasons for doing what I suggest to the government that it ought to do.
First, whatever is done ought to be consistent with whatever long term policy is likely to emerge. I think the denial of the sale of Home Oil would be consistent with long term policy. We cannot, however, simply deny the

February 18, 1971
Possible Takeover of Home Oil Company sale, particularly when the major owner is understood to be in financial difficulty, as perhaps was done in the case of Denison, without being prepared to give him an alternative. If we cannot find an alternative Canadian buyer for Home Oil I suggest to the government it should make a fair and reasonable bid for Home Oil and be prepared to purchase it.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: Under what statutory authority?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext:
There are several instruments in the Crown corporation field which could take on Home Oil. However, I do not think it would be good policy for us to suggest that this is the sort of thing the CDC should be expected to do. Very likely the CDC would be in a position to make a bid for Home Oil. I hope it would be. But it is not for the government to purchase an oil company and then press it upon the CDC. This would only confirm the fears of many persons that the CDC would be a basket for the dumping of companies purchased under political pressures. If we are prepared to purchase Home Oil, as I think we ought to do, we should be prepared to manage it as a public company. We should also be prepared to sell it to private Canadian interests if a good deal can be made, or be prepared to offer it to the CDC without any pressures.
It would seem to me that Panarctic Oils is a natural vehicle. I hope the minister is already in touch with that company with a view to keeping it advised of the situation and offering it the facilities of the government, financial and otherwise, to make a decent bid for Home Oil. Majority control of Panarctic does not he with the government, and if that company appears not to be interested, then Eldorado Mining Corporation is another natural company in this energy field. I hope the minister would use his influence to bring about the purchase by Eldorado of Home Oil.
There is no question that if the Canadian people come to own Home Oil they will have made an excellent purchase. It is a good company with good land and good oil reserves. It is not the company which is in difficulty but the owners. It has an international reputation and would be able to maintain itself in the international field where it has a demonstrated record of success. We would not be buying an enterprise as an act of last resort. We would be buying a viable, successful Canadian company which could become the building block or the cornerstone for a publicly-owned oil concern. We need a national or multi-national company in this field. We need to compete internationally in all spheres, not only in the resource field, though I think this would be a natural base for competition. I repeat that there are suitable vehicles available. But I do not believe in pressuring them into a purchase. If they are unable to bring themselves to a decision, then we should make it a separate government-owned Canadian company.
It seems to me that behind these proposals is a necessary decision on the part of the government. It is one thing to try to encourage Canadian companies to pur-

chase Home Oil; but if the owner finds a better deal elsewhere, then in the normal course of commercial practice he will accept the deal. It is one thing to suggest that Eldorado, Panarctic, Polymer or some other company in which the government has a major interest should get in touch with Home. But behind such a suggestion ought to be a clear pronouncement on the part of the government-I am prepared to see the government make such an announcement; some hon. members of the opposition are not-that under no circumstances will the government permit the sale of that company to foreign interests. I think that is the foundation block on which all other negotiations have to take place.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY PROJECTED TAKEOVER OF HOME OIL BY UNITED STATES COMPANY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

It is not pure faith at all. He has been trying to bring about a resolution of this dilemma in the voluntary way by finding Canadian buyers. This is the right way to go about it. It is true that we have a precedent in the Denison case, but that is a precedent which, I am sure we will all agree ought not to be repeated if it can be avoided. It is not good government policy to step in, in a retroactive sense, and deny the sale of a company. In some rare instances there is no time to wait for the policy that is coming forward, no time to wait for legislation, and in those circumstances I think the government has to weigh all the matters in balance. I think the government is doing this, and that the minister is doing the right thing in making every possible effort to resolve the issue.
What I am trying to say to the minister and to the government is that if those efforts fail, then I think the sense of the country is that we should take the next step and say that the company will not be sold abroad. Then, if we cannot find a consortium of Canadian companies to come forward, we will have to operate the company through the government's system.
Some hon. members had something to say about the north, but I do not want to get far into the question of the importance a company like Home Oil would have as a policy instrument in the matter of northern oil exploration and development. Canadians do want a vehicle of this kind; they want an opportunity to participate in resource development. They want this vehicle to reside in a successful company of which they can be proud.
It has been suggested that the regulations regarding development of the north should be changed because some uncertainty may have been created. There are billions of dollars going into northern exploration. Northern exploration has not ceased. The policies relating to exploration of the north were set in 1959, 1960, 1961 by a previous government. It makes no sense to have stayed with those regulations after Prudhoe Bay, and I agree it
February 18, 1971

is time they were changed. I believe that a company like Home Oil would be very suitable as a company participating in leasing, and leasing competitively, in the Canadian north. I would go further and say that a crown owned company ought to have devolved upon it a certain percentage of all the Crown lands that revert when one leases. That is taking a major step, and I would go that far.
The effort made by some members of the opposition to discuss the white paper on taxation is a subterfuge to conceal their policy. We have to face this question of what to do about Home Oil, and face it now.
